title: Li Lu: Compound Your Knowledge

reader_summary.source_label: From the episode notes — transcript not yet available
reader_summary.headline: Li Lu explains how to compound knowledge and capital while navigating markets and AI.
reader_summary.overview: This episode profiles Li Lu, a Chinese-born investor who started with simple balance sheet analysis and evolved to focus on businesses with lasting advantages. He shares six guiding principles from mentors like Graham, Buffett, and Munger, emphasizing a circle of competence and global purchasing power. The program details his specific investment history, including early mistakes and his views on artificial intelligence.

key_points.text: Li Lu states that if you can compound your knowledge sustainably, you can eventually compound your capital as well.
key_points.evidence_quote: And I always say, look, if you can compound your knowledge in a sustainable fashion, eventually you can compound your capital as well.

key_points.text: He measures wealth as a share of global purchasing power by owning great businesses in dynamic economies.
key_points.evidence_quote: His own sixth principle measures wealth as a share of global purchasing power.

key_points.text: Li Lu wants generative AI kept as a tool with a human in the loop rather than replacing human judgment.
key_points.evidence_quote: Near the end it takes up generative AI, which he wants kept a tool, with a human in the loop.

reader_summary.why_it_matters: Listeners learn how one investor evolved his strategy from simple statistics to owning great businesses with enduring advantages.

notes: We are delighted to share with you our audio program on Li Lu, founder and chairman of Himalaya Capital, part of the Great Investors podcast by Latticework. Each program in the series is an hour-long narrated profile of one investor, researched by the MOI Global team from the investor’s own lectures, writings and interviews. We make these programs so that members can learn how a great investor thinks and works, through the decisions he made and what he said about them at the time. Your feedback on what was useful, and on which investors to cover next, shapes what we produce. We start with who he is: Li Lu was the guest of honor at Columbia Business School’s thirty-sixth Graham & Dodd luncheon on October 5, 2026. He had attended a few of those luncheons as a student. He was born and raised in China, where, he said, there was not much of a private business or market economy at the time. From 1990 to 1996 he studied at Columbia and earned three degrees at once. There he went to a talk expecting a free lunch and heard Warren Buffett. He bought his first stock in 1993 and founded Himalaya Capital in 1997. In 2004 Charlie Munger became his partner. He started out knowing very little, he said, and learned his way from the simple to the complex. His first stocks were statistically cheap ones he could judge from a balance sheet, in the style of Benjamin Graham. Over the years he moved to good businesses, and then to businesses with enduring competitive advantages and long runways of growth. At the luncheon he put it as a rule: “And I always say, look, if you can compound your knowledge in a sustainable fashion, eventually you can compound your capital as well.” Every ten years, he said there, he finds himself a somewhat different person. Three of his six principles come from Graham. A share is a piece of a business. The market’s moods are there to be used, never obeyed. A margin of safety protects the downside. From Buffett comes the circle of competence, and he stresses where it ends as much as what lies inside it. He judges that he understands a business if he would buy more after its stock fell by half. From Munger comes a fisherman’s rule: go where hardly anyone is casting a line. His own sixth principle measures wealth as a share of global purchasing power. He keeps it by owning great businesses in the most dynamic economies, bought at good prices and held long enough for the value to be created. The program opens with those principles and then goes back to the start. It follows Timberland in the fall of 1998, when he read every complaint filed against the company. It covers the years he sold stocks short, which he called in 2013 one of the worst mistakes he had made. It has the Thanksgiving weekend of 2003 in Munger’s home library. It follows BYD from a trade magazine item around 2000 to a Berkshire Hathaway subsidiary’s agreement in September 2008 to buy 225 million new shares. Near the end it takes up generative AI, which he wants kept a tool, with a human in the loop. The program is built around his conversation at the luncheon with his host, Professor Tano Santos. The host asked what AI means for the equity analyst and how to protect a portfolio in a market top-heavy with a few giant companies. He also asked how to invest in China after the bust in its property market. Around that conversation the program sets what he said in English earlier, from a 2006 class at Columbia to a 2021 conversation with his old professor. It translates his talks in Mandarin, at Peking University in 2015 and to a gathering in Beijing in 2024. The complete program runs sixty-five minutes. Get the next program the day it comes out. Great Investors is on Apple, Spotify, and YouTube (or add the podcast feed to any app). The transcript is available for download to members only. Narrated by an AI voice. This is a public episode.  Search Home New Top Charts Sign In November 24 Li Lu: Compound Your Knowledge Great Investors 1h 5m We are delighted to share with you our audio program on Li Lu, founder and chairman of Himalaya Capital, part of the Great Investors podcast by Latticework. Each program in the series is an hour-long narrated profile of one investor, researched by the MOI Global team from the investor’s own lectures, writings and interviews. We make these programs so that members can learn how a great investor thinks and works, through the decisions he made and what he said about them at the time. Your feedback on what was useful, and on which investors to cover next, shapes what we produce. We start with who he is:

 Li Lu was the guest of honor at Columbia Business School’s thirty-sixth Graham & Dodd luncheon on October 5, 2026. He had attended a few of those luncheons as a student. He was born and raised in China, where, he said, there was not much of a private business or market economy at the time. From 1990 to 1996 he studied at Columbia and earned three degrees at once. There he went to a talk expecting a free lunch and heard Warren Buffett. He bought his first stock in 1993 and founded Himalaya Capital in 1997. In 2004 Charlie Munger became his partner.

 He started out knowing very little, he said, and learned his way from the simple to the complex. His first stocks were statistically cheap ones he could judge from a balance sheet, in the style of Benjamin Graham. Over the years he moved to good businesses, and then to businesses with enduring competitive advantages and long runways of growth. At the luncheon he put it as a rule: “And I always say, look, if you can compound your knowledge in a sustainable fashion, eventually you can compound your capital as well.” Every ten years, he said there, he finds himself a somewhat different person.

 Three of his six principles come from Graham. A share is a piece of a business. The market’s moods are there to be used, never obeyed. A margin of safety protects the downside. From Buffett comes the circle of competence, and he stresses where it ends as much as what lies inside it. He judges that he understands a business if he would buy more after its stock fell by half. From Munger comes a fisherman’s rule: go where hardly anyone is casting a line. His own sixth principle measures wealth as a share of global purchasing power. He keeps it by owning great businesses in the most dynamic economies, bought at good prices and held long enough for the value to be created.

 The program opens with those principles and then goes back to the start. It follows Timberland in the fall of 1998, when he read every complaint filed against the company. It covers the years he sold stocks short, which he called in 2013 one of the worst mistakes he had made. It has the Thanksgiving weekend of 2003 in Munger’s home library. It follows BYD from a trade magazine item around 2000 to a Berkshire Hathaway subsidiary’s agreement in September 2008 to buy 225 million new shares. Near the end it takes up generative AI, which he wants kept a tool, with a human in the loop.

 The program is built around his conversation at the luncheon with his host, Professor Tano Santos. The host asked what AI means for the equity analyst and how to protect a portfolio in a market top-heavy with a few giant companies. He also asked how to invest in China after the bust in its property market. Around that conversation the program sets what he said in English earlier, from a 2006 class at Columbia to a 2021 conversation with his old professor. It translates his talks in Mandarin, at Peking University in 2015 and to a gathering in Beijing in 2024.

 The complete program runs sixty-five minutes.

 Get the next program the day it comes out. Great Investors is on Apple, Spotify, and YouTube (or add the podcast feed to any app).

 The transcript is available for download to members only.

 Narrated by an AI voice.
